memoryText: For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Ezekiel 18:32 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is both a word of judgment and a word of love. It stands at the end of the chapter about individual responsibility, and it is God’s own explanation of why he calls people to repentance.

“I have no pleasure in the death of anyone.” This is a statement about God’s heart. Many people think of God as someone who is eager to punish. This verse says the opposite. When someone dies in sin, God takes no delight in it. Judgment is real, and God carries it out. But it is his “strange work,” as Isaiah calls it. It is not his joy.

“Declares the Lord GOD.” The title used here, Adonai Yahweh, is the strongest possible way to say that the Master and covenant God is speaking. The statement is not a casual opinion. It is a sworn declaration.

“So turn, and live.” This is the invitation. The command to turn is a command to repent, to change direction. The result is life. Notice the simplicity: turn, and live. The exiles had been saying that their situation was hopeless. God says the way is open. Turn.

The Christian reads this verse in light of the cross. God’s desire for people to live is shown in the fact that he sent his Son. “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.” In Christ, the call to turn is also a call to come to the one who has taken the death we deserved.

Say this verse for yourself when you are tempted to think that God is only waiting to condemn you. Say it for others when you pray for them. God does not want anyone to die. Turn, and live.
weekInReview: This week you prayed three Songs of Ascents: Psalm 122, the joy of going up to the house of the LORD, and Psalms 123 and 126, the servant’s eyes on his master and the promise that those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy. You read Ezekiel 18, in which God rejects the proverb about sour grapes, declares that each soul is accountable, and says that he has no pleasure in the death of anyone. You read about the sword drawn against Jerusalem, God’s search for someone to stand in the breach, and the death of Ezekiel’s wife as a sign of the grief to come. You surveyed the oracles against the nations: Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and its proud king, and Egypt with its crocodile and fallen cedar. The week taught that each person is responsible before God, that he delights in repentance, and that pride before him is brought low.
reflectionQuestions: Ezekiel 18 insists that no one can blame the past for their present. Is there an area where you have been tempted to say, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes”?
God looked for someone to stand in the breach and found none. Who is someone you could stand in the breach for through prayer this week?
Psalm 126 says that those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy. What is something you are sowing in tears right now, and what would it look like to trust the harvest?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he has no pleasure in anyone’s death.
Thank him for the cross where he stood in the breach for you.
